video_title: Everyone’s Bracing for a Crash. The Economy Says Otherwise.
gist: Franklin Templeton Institute market strategist Chris Gallipo argues that crash fears are misplaced because earnings growth — broad across EM, US small caps and AI adopters — is strong and set to continue through 2028, with the S&P up ~13.5% YTD despite a 100bp rise in long rates, oil above $100 and a new Fed hiking cycle. He rejects the AI-bubble comparison to 2000 on valuation grounds (S&P ~21x forward, Nvidia ~20x), flags that corporate AI ROI disclosures are under-appreciated, and names peak rate-of-change in earnings in 2027 and an extended Fed hiking cycle (6–7 hikes) as the two real equity risks.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is up about 13.5% year-to-date in 2026 despite long rates backing up ~100 basis points, oil rising from ~$65 to above $100, and a starting multiple of ~22.5x on January 1, with four or five 4–9% pullbacks along the way.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Equities absorbed a rate and oil shock that would normally derail a rally — evidence that earnings, not macro headlines, are driving the tape.

insights.claim: Gallipo holds that earnings growth is by far the most important variable for stocks, that H1 2026 earnings came in well ahead of Street forecasts, and that strong earnings growth looks set to continue through calendar 2026 into 2027 and 2028.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: A multi-year earnings runway supports staying invested through headline-driven pullbacks; watch Q3 reporting season (starting in early October) as the next test.
insights.quote: Earnings matter. Period. End of story. And earnings have been fabulous.

insights.claim: Stock market crashes rarely happen on their own; they are usually Fed-induced — the Fed takes rates too high, holds them too long and breaks something — or caused by an unforecastable black swan like COVID, and recessions occur roughly once a decade.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Track Fed policy overshoot rather than sentiment as the crash trigger; persistent recession calls have a poor base rate.
insights.quote: The world doesn't end that often. The stock market just doesn't crash on its own. It's usually Fed induced or Fed related

insights.claim: Market rotation over the past two years — broader participation beyond a narrow set of leaders — is bullish rather than a sign of weakness; when semiconductors unwound, the overall index did not flinch and simply rotated into other areas.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Breadth expansion argues against a top; sector rotations are opportunities to rebalance rather than signals to de-risk wholesale.

themes.theme: Fed hikes, oil and sticky inflation

insights.claim: After the Fed's first rate hike of the new cycle, Gallipo expects one or two more hikes, which he believes the economy and stock market can absorb; he notes the Fed has hiked once and stopped only once in history.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Base case is a short, measured hiking cycle — not the kind that 'breaks something' — so rate risk is manageable for equities.

insights.claim: Core inflation is running around 3%, about 50% above the Fed's 2% target, and the current rate hikes are primarily an attempt by the Fed to re-establish its credibility; Gallipo thinks the Fed would prefer to pause if demand weakens and gives it cover.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Hikes are credibility-driven rather than overheating-driven, which suggests a reaction function likely to stop early on any demand softness.
insights.quote: The raising the raising of rates here honestly Maggie is is is an attempt to reestablish their credibility

insights.claim: Current inflation is mainly a supply-side shock, so raising rates by 100 basis points would do nothing to the price of oil, diesel or gasoline; the economy is not overheating even though inflation has been sticky for five years.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Monetary tightening is a blunt tool against energy-driven inflation — an aggressive Fed would hurt growth without fixing prices, reinforcing the case for a measured Fed.
insights.quote: They could raise rates by 100 basis points will do nothing to the price of oil or diesel or gas.

insights.claim: Oil would need to trade appreciably above $100 and hold there for about six months to become a real macro problem, but higher oil already bleeds into core inflation through transport costs — truckers and railroads shipping goods from ports raise prices in a negative reinforcing loop.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Watch the duration of $100+ oil, not just the level; transport-cost pass-through is the channel into core inflation.

insights.claim: The two primary risks for equities are (1) the peak rate of change in earnings growth — 2027 faces tough first-half comparisons — and (2) a Fed that hikes six or seven times rather than once or twice.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Equities are a rate-of-change business: the risk is decelerating earnings growth, not falling earnings — watch 2027 comps and the number of hikes priced.
insights.quote: the equity business is a rate of change business.

insights.claim: The Magnificent 7's forward multiple is well below its 10-year median, which could mean the market is already pricing peak rate of change in earnings — low multiples on Nvidia or Microsoft may reflect peak-EPS expectations rather than cheapness.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: A low multiple on mega-cap tech is ambiguous — it can be a value signal or a peak-growth warning; hard to tell in real time.

insights.claim: AI leaders are not in a bubble on valuation grounds: Google, Microsoft and Nvidia trade at multiples below the S&P 500, Nvidia is around 20x earnings, and the S&P trades ~21x current-year and ~19x next-year earnings, versus Cisco at ~100x and the S&P at ~30x at the March 2000 peak.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Valuation comparisons argue against shorting AI megacaps on a dot-com analogy; the risk lies elsewhere (circular financing, capex/FCF).
insights.quote: you can't tell me it's a bubble when when the the big companies in the space, you pick Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia. Well, maybe not Amazon, but the other three trade at multiples below the tape.

insights.claim: The genuine concerns in AI are the circular nature of the financing and the hyperscalers having blown through free cash flow conversion over roughly the last year, which Gallipo says nobody saw coming.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Monitor hyperscaler FCF and vendor-financing loops as the real AI stress points rather than P/E multiples.

insights.claim: Semiconductor stocks went into 'complete speculation mode' with a parabolic, 2000-like move around Q2 2026, then were clobbered and reset — an example of the stock market 'taking out its own trash' amid leveraged ETFs, margin and options that make speculation easy.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Localized speculative blowoffs can flush out without breaking the broad market; leveraged momentum pockets are where the wrecking ball hits.
insights.quote: That was a casino, not investing.

themes.theme: AI ROI showing up in earnings

insights.claim: In Q2 2026 roughly 25 S&P 500 companies gave a discernible ROI for their use of AI, and management teams are increasingly volunteering AI efficiency, margin accretion and net-income accretion figures on earnings calls — contrary to the skeptic narrative that nobody is implementing AI profitably.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: AI adopters across all industries (not just AI vendors) could see margin upside; track the count of companies quantifying AI ROI in Q3 reports.
insights.quote: That that's the first inning of a ninninging game.

insights.claim: Walmart management said it can grow revenue over the next five years at the same rate as the prior five years without adding headcount, and that shoppers using Walmart's in-app AI tool spend about 35% more than those who don't.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: AI is delivering both cost leverage and revenue uplift at a mainstream retailer — a template for margin expansion in non-tech sectors (speaker advised verifying the exact figures).

insights.claim: Companies are not rushing to lay people off due to AI but are more cautious about adding headcount where in-house technology can perform the function, which likely explains part of the 'low hiring, low firing' job market of the last one to two years.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: AI is showing up as suppressed hiring rather than layoffs — supportive for margins but a headwind for new-entrant employment and a policy problem.

insights.claim: Gallipo sees AI-safety calls to slow development as a risk to AI valuations mainly if government regulation is layered on, but says no slowdown in AI deployment has been observed and he doubts government regulation is the right mechanism.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Regulation is the tail risk that could re-rate AI growth assumptions; absent that, safety debate is noise for now.

themes.theme: EM and small caps lead earnings

insights.claim: Emerging markets have had the strongest global earnings power for the last year and a half, likely continuing into next year, driven primarily by South Korea and Taiwan (Taiwan Semi, Samsung, SK Hynix) rather than China, with breadth in industrials, healthcare and materials too.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: EM leadership is a Korea/Taiwan semis story first — EM exposure is partly a correlated AI/semis bet.
insights.quote: It's not really China. It's South Korea, Taiwan are the two prime prime drivers.

insights.claim: US small caps have the strongest forward earnings growth rate of change and two years of strong estimate revisions likely continuing into 2027, supported by real GDP running above 2% versus a ~1.8% long-term trend, but they are more rate-sensitive because many carry floating-rate debt.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Small-cap outperformance can continue on earnings, but a further rise in long rates / curve is the key risk to the trade.

insights.claim: Buying energy names or utilities as an 'AI-adjacent' power-grid play on top of semis and hyperscalers largely replicates the same beta, since those stocks tend to trade in the same direction over time.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: Check factor correlation before adding AI power plays as diversification — they're the same trade.
insights.quote: just be advised that you're you're replicating beta over different.

insights.claim: A reusable test for any position: 'If I didn't own this stock today, would I buy it here?' — if yes after a drawdown, hold or add; if a stock has gone vertical, wait for better risk/reward even if fundamentals are good.
insights.speaker: Chris Gallipo (Franklin Templeton Institute)
insights.so_what: A simple emotional check for trimming parabolic winners and adding to fundamentally intact losers during volatility.
insights.quote: if I didn't own this stock today, would I buy it here?
